title: Fizik Versor 2 MTB Shoe Review: Trail Tools – John Watson
content:
John’s been wearing the Fizik Versor 2 MTB shoe for a few months in the Southern Rockies, on long days out and trail-work outings. He’s got some thoughts in a quick review…

Shoes, like saddles, grips, and gloves, are a highly subjective product to review. Everyone’s feet are different. Some are bony, skinny, and prone to injury, while others are bigger, wider, and more robust. Mine are the former. Long, skinny, and bony. So when a shoe touts a secure fit with lightweight protection like the Fizik Versor 2, I’m interested. But before we get into that…

Fizik Versor 2 Quick Hits

  • $149.99
  • Size 36 – 48
  • 980 grams for size 47 shown here
  • Black (shown) or white
  • SPD cleat compatible
  • Also available as a flat pedal
  • Vibram sole
  • Ripstop fabric: woven fabric resistant to tearing and ripping
  • Laced closure for the BOA-averse riders

Construction

The Versor 2 features a stretchy sleeve to keep rocks, dirt, and debris out of the shoe. It uses a lace-up closure, rather than Velcro straps or BOA systems common in many modern shoes. The Vibram sole and outsole cover a ripstop woven fabric on the upper, designed to resist abrasion. These are stout, heavy-duty shoes, built for trail riding. Yet my size 47 weighs only 980 grams (2.15 lbs) for the pair, including cleats. I have to install my cleats really far back, and Fizik’s cleat beds always allow for the correct positioning for my bike fit.

Fit and Feel

The first time I laced up the Versor 2, I had to mess a bit with the lace tension. Laces tend to stretch as you ride, particularly on new shoes, so leaving them too tight is better than too loose. For someone who has long, bony feet, the shoes felt super secure and comfy. In fact, they’re the most comfortable off-the-bike shoe I’ve worn in terms of sole support and walking comfort.

Off the Bike: Trail Work

This summer ended with a flood of rain, and with it came a slew of downed trees and washouts in need of repair. All of my rides require some form of trail work these days, with either a packable pocket chainsaw or the big boss of trail saws, the Hunkenr that Travis reviewed. For bigger jobs, I’ll pack in my Trail Boss tools and climb up to the area in need of work.

Not only are the Versor 2 shoes incredibly supportive during this sort of work, but they also grip incredibly well, even after getting wet. Using a McLeod tool or Rogue hoe, flinging dirt and rocks out of the way, the elastic sleeve around the opening kept my shoes free of debris. I never felt the shoes rub up on the heel, which would cause blisters to form during a long day’s work.

The rubber outer and Vibram soles withstood a good amount of abuse while maintaining their tread pattern. Overall, in terms of comfort and durability, I’d give these a high rating, if it weren’t for a single incident I had last month.

On the Bike: Into the Rocks

On a ride with friends in the Sierra, I hucked my Significant Other Ded Rek into a rocky chute, only to be greeted with a giant piece of rock straight to the shin. Luckily, the impact happened under a pair of socks, which the rock cut into, along with my Versor 2 shoes. The little gash on the left foot shown in these photos came from this impact. I’d never, ever cut shoes like that on rocks, having kicked and shinned a number of sharp impacts over the years.

All this to say, I was shocked. The cut went clear through the ripstop and the hard plastic shank of the shoe. Who knows what damage this impact would have done to other shoes I’ve worn over the past few years, and my shin certainly took the brunt of the impact, with a scab that continuously fell victim to other trail abrasions and took forever to heal. But it did cause pause.

These two photos show the interference with the top of my foot and the laces wing at the top of the shoe…

Versor 2 Achilles

As I said in the beginning of this review, shoe reviews are hella subjective. What bothers my feet might not bother yours. But one thing I found was that, in order to have the correct tension with the laces to form a secure, snug fit, the little wing where the top lace loops through dug into my foot. After a big day of climbing, it was noticeably tender, and the following day, the spot would be sore when I put the shoes back on.

What the Versor 2 Gets Right vs. Wrong

Durability, feel, support, and looks are all where the Versor 2 lands a dang near perfect rating. However, the closure system and the hard laces digging into my foot make me question how much longer I’ll want to wear them. But YMMV, and not everyone’s foot profile is the same. Placing that critique aside, I can’t think of a more bomber shoe I’ve owned in recent years, where a shoe is comfortable both on big backcountry days and after a full afternoon of trail work.

Working on trails is a full-body effort, and our feet can withstand a lot of abuse. The Versor 2 nailed both on- and off-bike feel, and this pair has endured a good amount of abuse. Aside from a single tear and a subjective fit issue with the shoe’s silhouette, they’ve been bomber.

Pros

  • Elastic cuff enclosure keeps debris out
  • Vibram sole is hella grippy
  • Exceptionally comfortable in terms of sole support
  • Cleat install is easy, offering plenty of fore/aft adjustment
  • Price ain’t bad. Not cheap. Not expensive.

Cons

  • Fit issues (for me, but perhaps not for you)
  • Durability questions from a single rock strike
